explanation: [[kw:Simple interest]] is calculated only on the original principal each period.
[[kw:Compound interest]] calculates interest on the principal plus any previously earned interest.
Compounding results in a higher total return because interest earns interest.
[[kw:Future value (FV)]] or compound amount is the total value at the end of the investment/loan.

explanation: Compounding frequency determines how often interest is calculated and added to the principal.
[[kw:Annually]]: once per year.
[[kw:Semiannually]]: twice per year (every 6 months).
[[kw:Quarterly]]: four times per year (every 3 months).
[[kw:Monthly]]: twelve times per year.
[[kw:Daily]]: 360 times per year (ordinary) or 365 (exact) depending on the convention.
[[imp:More frequent compounding = higher effective rate and future value.]]

formulaCard.title: Compound Amount (Future Value) Formula
notes: n = total number of compounding periods.

explanation: Manual calculation: start with the principal (PV). For each period, multiply by (1 + i), where i is the periodic rate.
After n periods, the future value is $$FV = PV \times (1 + i)^n$$.
Alternatively, calculate interest period by period: add interest to the old balance to get the new balance.
Compound interest = FV - PV.
[[imp:The factor (1+i) is called the accumulation factor; raising it to the n-th power gives the growth over n periods.]]

visuals.caption: Each period: Interest = Balance × i; new balance = old balance + interest.

blocks.title: 4. Using Future Value Table

challengeCorner.prompt: An investment of $3,200 earns 8% compounded quarterly for 2 years. Use the formula or table to find FV (factor (1.02)^8 = 1.17166).

visuals.caption: Factor = (1 + i)^n. Multiply principal by factor to get FV.
visuals.title: Future Value of $1 Table (Excerpt)

explanation: A [[kw:future value of $1 table]] provides pre-calculated values of $(1 + i)^n$ for common i and n.
Steps: 1. Calculate n and i for the given compounding frequency. 2. Look up the factor at the intersection of i (row) and n (column). 3. Multiply the principal (PV) by the factor to get FV.
This method is simpler than manual exponentiation.
Tables often have row labels for periodic interest rate and column labels for number of periods.
[[imp:Always ensure i and n correspond to the same compounding frequency.]]

formulaCard.title: FV Using Table
notes: Find i (periodic rate) and n (total periods) before using the table.

discoveryHook.scenario: Two banks offer 8% interest, but one compounds annually, the other quarterly. Which is better? The quarterly compounding yields an [[kw:effective annual rate (APY)]] higher than 8%. The formula: APY = (1 + periodic rate)^periods per year - 1. For 8% quarterly: APY = (1.02)^4 - 1 ≈ 8.24%.

teacherCues: Define APY (Annual Percentage Yield) as the true annual interest rate accounting for compounding.
Effective rate = (1 + i)^m - 1, where m = compounding periods per year.

blocks.title: 5. Effective Rate (APY)

questions.prompt: Nominal rate 10%, compounded semiannually. Find APY (as decimal, 4 decimals).
If APY = 0.0824, what is the nominal rate if compounding is quarterly? (Hint: (1+i)^4 = 1.0824, so i = 1.0824^(1/4) - 1 ≈ 0.02, then nominal = 4 × 0.02 = 8%). (number only, no % sign)

explanation: The [[kw:Annual Percentage Yield (APY)]] or effective annual rate is the true interest rate after taking compounding into account.
Formula: $$APY = \left(1 + \frac{r}{m}\right)^m - 1$$ where $r$ = nominal annual rate, $m$ = compounding periods per year.
Alternatively: $APY = (1 + i)^m - 1$ where $i$ = periodic rate.
APY allows comparison of investments with different compounding frequencies.
[[imp:APY is always greater than or equal to the nominal rate if compounding is more frequent than annual.]]

formulaCard.title: Effective Annual Rate (APY)
notes: m = number of compounding periods per year.
Use APY to compare investments with different compounding frequencies.
